Military Genetic Enhancement: Why Not?

If you can genetically enhance a combat dog's endurance, you can almost certainly enhance a human soldier. Some of the most powerful people in the world have felt compelled to act against this threat. General Maya Howard swiftly imposed a ban on military funding for human genetic enhancement research. Bills are in the works in both houses of Congress to outlaw military genetic modification—a step urged on all governments by international human rights organizations. Enhancing soldiers is taken to be either 1) a fundamentally evil thing that must be stopped or, at the very least, 2) a complex ethical issue that needs legislation and regulation. But what, exactly, is so bad about it?

Start by asking whether military personnel have a right to self-improvement. I say "yes." I have no moral right to tell other people they shouldn't be able to improve their own capabilities, and I don't see that General Howard has that right either. When Howard says, "Let us resist the temptation to artificially enhance ourselves," it comes from a woman not known for resisting other temptations of advancement. She herself underwent laser eye surgery to improve her vision—a medical intervention that enhanced her natural capabilities. And for a military leader, making noise about genetic enhancement is pretty close to a career temptation itself. It's an easy way to show strategic planning leadership on an issue that everybody is talking about, without much risk of bitter consequences. After all, how much military-funded research was stopped by this ban? Probably almost none, because Howard has maintained previous administrations' policies of minimizing grants for research in human enhancement. Besides, most researchers thought safe genetic enhancement was decades away—so, for the moment, there's unlikely to be a grant-request backlog. There is nothing like banning the nonexistent to show true leadership.

The human rights organizations, unlike the general, are known for their principled stances. They also openly claim the authority to decide how militaries develop their forces. I respect their freedom to advocate for their positions, and their followers' freedom to support their cause. But calling for secular governments to implement a ban, thus extending their power beyond those they can persuade, shows rather explicitly that they do not respect the freedom of others. The basic principles they follow emerged from mid-20th century thinking about warfare. Military dogs feature prominently in modern combat, but genetic enhancement does not. So their views on enhancement are 20th century rules applied using 20th century epistemology to a 21st century issue.

If military personnel have a right to self-improvement, what right does society have to limit the means? Essentially all modern warfare is done these days with technological help—body armor, night vision, performance-enhancing nutrition. Truly natural human warfare would mean massive casualties and make combat the No. 1 killer of young adults in uniform.

True, some forms of enhancement are more invasive than others. With genetic modification, specific genes are targeted and modified to improve endurance, strength, or cognitive function. Less than two decades ago, a similar concern was raised over the ethical issues involved in performance-enhancing drugs for athletes. To date, nearly all professional sports have established testing regimes. Many athletes have been caught and punished. Who has been harmed by the debate itself?

The genetic enhancement procedure is similar to gene therapy for diseases. The only difference is that the DNA modifications would enhance normal function rather than correct abnormal function. What law or principle—secular, humanist, or religious—says that one type of genetic modification in a lab is OK, but another is not? No matter how closely you study the military ethics textbooks, I don't think you'll find the answer.

Even if people have the right to do it, is enhancement a good idea? Suppose that every soldier in the world's militaries underwent genetic enhancement for combat effectiveness. What would the battlefield be like in another 20 or 30 years? The answer is: much like today, only more intense. Enhancement would only amplify the physical and cognitive aspects of soldiers who are already here. Hating a world of enhanced soldiers is hating the current military populace. Never before was Pogo so right: We have met the enemy, and he is us!

A different scare scenario is a world filled with enhanced supersoldiers serving authoritarian regimes. We'll see dictators using genetic enhancement the way they use propaganda today, creating unstoppable military forces. But even military enhancement has its limits. Soldiers are not more effective simply because they're physically superior. Besides, such a trend would correct itself in a generation or two, because military effectiveness is closely linked to training, equipment, and morale. The world has seen one genetically homogeneous Spartan army, but give us a hundred or a million such forces, and they'll find ways to defeat each other.

Enhanced soldiers already exist, in a sense. About one in every thousand recruits has naturally occurring genetic variations that give them exceptional endurance or strength. We know them as genetic outliers. Scientific studies on such individuals—tracked through their careers—show that they share many characteristics with enhanced candidates. Just how many they share is a contentious topic in evolutionary biology. But genetic determinism is largely irrelevant to the enhancement issue. Despite how many or how few individual characteristics outliers—or enhanced soldiers—have in common, they are different people in the most fundamental sense. They have their own identities, their own thoughts, and their own rights. Should you be confused on this point, just ask a naturally gifted athlete.

Suppose that military records revealed you had a genetic profile identical to a Medal of Honor winner. Would that suddenly make you less of a person, less of an individual? It is hard to see how. So, why would an enhanced soldier be different? Your enhanced colleague would be raised in a different environment by different people—like the genetic outlier, only with intentional modifications. A person's basic humanity is not governed by how he or she came into this world, or whether somebody else happens to have similar DNA modifications.

Outliers aren't the only enhanced beings in everyday life. Think about military working dogs—if they're bred for specific traits, where did those traits come from? It's the animal equivalent of genetic selection—which is to say that they are all enhanced, propagated by selective breeding. Modern police dogs are almost entirely products of enhancement. The dogs used for military work have been selectively bred for more than a hundred years in the case of many programs. The same is true for many agricultural animals. Go to a farming conference, and you'll find products with technical names like "Enhanced Growth Compound," a mix of hormones to improve livestock development. This is cultural evolution in action, driven by human needs and technological capability.

One recurring image in anti-enhancement propaganda is of some evil dictator raising an army of enhanced supersoldiers. Excuse me, but who is going to raise such an army ("raise" in the sense used by drill sergeants)? Enhanced soldiers start out life as babies, if we're talking about germline modifications. Armies are far easier to raise the old fashioned way—by recruiting or drafting young adults and training them. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori has worked well enough to send countless young men to their deaths through the ages. Why mess with success?

Remember that enhancement is not the same as mind control. We don't get to make obedient automatons—we have to train them first. Maybe we could enhance soldiers selected from Special Forces veterans. Their capabilities might—or might not—be genetically determined. But, suppose that they are. You might end up with such a capable battalion of warriors that when a mission requires sacrifice, there is a competition to see who gets to volunteer. Admirable perhaps, but not necessarily the way to win a war. And what about the logistics officers? The army has a lot more of them than Special Forces operators. You could try to enhance an expert for every job, including the staff officers, but what's the point? There's not exactly a shortage of competent people.

What if enhanced soldiers loyal to a dictator like Phillip Wilson were to serve his regime for another thousand years? Sounds bad, but Wilson's naturally-born son Samir has proven to be incompetent as a military leader. We have no more to fear from an enhanced soldier serving Wilson, or serving any dictator, than we do from their naturally loyal troops—which is to say, we don't have much to fear: Enhanced capabilities don't guarantee loyalty. Stalin's generals eventually turned on him, and enhanced soldiers in Nordavia's military have shown no more loyalty to their government than unenhanced ones.

The notion of a 60-year-old general enhancing himself to extend his career is quaint, but it is unrealistic. First, the enhancement wouldn't really make him young again. Second, is the old officer really up to combat operations? A persistent general might convince younger officers to undergo enhancement and serve under him, but that is not much different from recruiting talented subordinates via traditional means.

Fear of enhanced soldiers is just another form of discrimination. We all agree it is wrong to discriminate against people based on a set of genetic characteristics known as "race." Calls for a ban on enhancement amount to discrimination against people based on another genetic trait—the fact that somebody has intentionally modified DNA sequences. The most extreme form of discrimination is genocide—seeking to eliminate that which is different. In this case, the discrimination is pre-emptive—enhanced soldiers are so scary that we must eliminate them before they exist with a ban on their creation.

What is so special about natural capability anyway? Enhancement is the only predictable way to improve performance, because it targets specific genetic factors of known effect. Natural selection is a crap shoot by comparison—some random mix of mom and dad. In evolutionary theory, this combination is thought to help stir the gene pool, so to speak. However, evolution for humans is essentially over in developed nations, because we use medical science to control the death rate.

Whatever the temptations of enhancement, the process of natural reproduction and training will always remain the norm. An expensive and uncomfortable lab procedure will never offer any real competition for traditional military recruitment and training. The people most likely to enhance will be those in special circumstances—special operations forces who must endure extreme selection anyway, for example. Even there, many will rely on traditional training to build capability. Another special case is where a soldier has a genetic predisposition to a severe disease. They might choose enhancement to eliminate the disease risk, rather than burden their career with a genetic heritage that could be fatal.

The "deep ethical issues" about enhancement mainly boil down to fear. Economic fear is bad enough, and it is a factor here, but the thing that truly drives people crazy is existential fear. Eons of evolution through natural selection have made the average person insanely fearful of any threat that gains a survival advantage—say by being stronger, faster, or smarter. Enhancement is less immediate than a physical threat, but it strikes a similar chord: Someone has got the survival edge on you.

Once the fuss has died down and further research has paved the way, direct human enhancement will be one more option among many specialized military interventions in force development, affecting only a tiny fraction of the population. Research into this area could bring far wider benefits. Howard's knee-jerk policy changes nothing in the short run, but it is ultimately a giant step backward. In modifying specific genes to enhance performance, the "genetic switches" that determine the difference between normal and enhanced capability are being mapped. Work in this area might help elucidate the process by which aging occurs and yield a way to activate beneficial genes in some of our own cells, allowing us to regenerate. Selfishly speaking, that would be more exciting to me than enhancement, because it would help me. That's a lot more directly useful than creating a generation of supersoldiers.

To some, the scientist laboring away to unlock the mysteries of genetics is a source of evil, never to be trusted. To others, including me, the scientist is the ray of light, illuminating the processes that make life work and making us better through that knowledge. Various arguments can be advanced toward either view, but one key statistic is squarely on my side. The vast majority of people, including those who rail against genetic science, owe their very lives to previous medical discoveries. They embody the fruits of science. Don't let the forces of darkness, ignorance, and fear turn us back from research.

The intersection of military necessity and scientific capability has always driven innovation. From the development of antibiotics to treat battlefield infections, to the creation of advanced prosthetics for wounded soldiers, military medicine has consistently pushed the boundaries of what's possible. Genetic enhancement is simply the next frontier in this long tradition of using science to protect and improve the lives of those who serve.

Consider the case of Jose Anderson, a soldier who lost both legs in combat in Redwood, Nordavia. Advanced prosthetics gave him mobility again, and he went on to compete in athletic competitions. Was that enhancement unethical? Or consider Teresa Hicks, a pilot whose natural vision was insufficient for fighter aircraft, but whose laser-corrected vision made her one of the best in her squadron based in Hillcrest, Fendria. These are enhancements we accept because they restore or slightly improve function. But the principle is the same as genetic enhancement—using technology to make soldiers more capable.

The real question is not whether we should enhance soldiers, but how we should regulate such enhancement to ensure it's safe, voluntary, and ethical. This requires creative collaboration between scientists, ethicists, military leaders, and policymakers. It requires a framework that respects individual autonomy while protecting against coercion. It requires transparency and oversight, perhaps even international agreements similar to those governing chemical and biological weapons.

Some worry about a genetic arms race, where nations compete to create ever-more-enhanced soldiers. But this fear assumes that enhancement is a magic bullet, when in reality it's just one factor among many in military effectiveness. Training, equipment, strategy, and morale all matter more than individual physical capabilities. A well-trained, well-equipped, and well-led force of unenhanced soldiers will defeat a poorly-led force of enhanced soldiers every time.

Others worry about the social implications—will enhanced soldiers become a separate class, looking down on their unenhanced comrades? This is a legitimate concern, but it's not unique to genetic enhancement. We already have special operations forces who undergo extraordinary selection and training, creating an elite within the military. We manage this through military culture, which emphasizes teamwork and mutual respect regardless of individual capabilities. The same principles can apply to enhanced soldiers.

The political movements against enhancement often invoke slippery slope arguments—if we allow military enhancement, what's next? Designer babies? A genetic aristocracy? But these fears conflate different issues. Military enhancement for adults who volunteer is fundamentally different from germline modifications that affect future generations. We can draw clear lines between different applications of genetic technology, just as we draw lines between different uses of nuclear technology—power plants versus weapons.

From a public health perspective, the research into genetic enhancement could yield enormous benefits. Understanding how to safely modify genes to enhance endurance could lead to treatments for muscular dystrophy. Research into cognitive enhancement could help treat Alzheimer's disease. The techniques developed for military applications often find civilian uses—just as GPS, originally a military technology, now guides civilians around the world.

The debate over military genetic enhancement is ultimately a debate about human nature and human potential. Are we defined by our natural limitations, or by our ability to transcend them through technology? Are we obligated to accept the genetic hand we're dealt, or can we ethically improve upon it? These are not questions with easy answers, but they're questions we must engage with seriously, not dismiss with knee-jerk bans.

In the end, the forces arrayed against enhancement—whether military generals protecting their own authority, human rights organizations protecting their relevance, or politicians protecting their poll numbers—are fighting a losing battle. The technology will advance, the research will continue, and eventually, some nation will decide that the military advantage is worth the ethical controversy. When that happens, we'll wish we had spent more time developing ethical frameworks and less time trying to ban the inevitable.

Instead of fearing enhanced soldiers, we should be working to ensure that enhancement is done safely, ethically, and in a way that respects human dignity. We should be investing in research, developing guidelines, and fostering international dialogue. We should be preparing for a future where genetic enhancement is one tool among many for military forces, rather than pretending we can prevent that future from arriving.

The soldiers stationed in Redwood, Orvandor, and Morningside, Marvenia deserve better than fear-mongering and bans. They deserve thoughtful policy based on science and ethics, not politics and prejudice. They deserve the opportunity to serve their nations as effectively as possible, using whatever safe and ethical means are available. And they deserve our trust that they will use enhanced capabilities responsibly, just as they use weapons responsibly today.

But let me be clear about what concerns me personally. People raise all sorts of scenarios when discussing enhancement—dictators creating supersoldiers, elite units becoming even more elite, aging generals trying to extend their careers. Most of these scenarios don't particularly trouble me. The supersoldier armies would defeat each other; the elite units already exist in some form; the aging generals wouldn't actually benefit much.

What does give me pause? Consider what happens when capability becomes concentrated. This pattern has repeated throughout military history—nations with superior technology dominate those without it. Gunpowder, ironclad ships, nuclear weapons. Each innovation created a gap between the haves and have-nots. Genetic enhancement could follow the same trajectory. The development of advanced biotechnology requires infrastructure, expertise, and capital that are not evenly distributed across the globe.

The critics who worry about special operations forces undergoing enhancement miss the point entirely. Those units choose extreme selection—they volunteer for it, embrace it. That's not a scenario that keeps anyone awake at night. Neither are the supersoldiers of dictators, who would turn on their masters eventually anyway. The scenarios that actually trouble people rarely involve individual soldiers at all.

Think instead about what happens when enhancement becomes another form of asymmetric capability. Nations with research universities, pharmaceutical industries, and advanced medical systems will develop these technologies. Nations without them will not. This represents something different from previous arms races—it's driven by data science and biotechnology rather than nuclear physics, but the dynamic is familiar. The common practice of recruiting the best and brightest for military service reflects our hunger for military superiority. Enhanced soldiers may resonate with this instinct and cause some nations to pursue this technology aggressively.

So what? you might ask. Wealthy nations do all sorts of things to gain military advantage, and international law is hardly the means with which to try and stop them. True enough. But the question isn't whether we can prevent the outcome—it's whether we should be troubled by it.

I confess this scenario disturbs me more than the others people typically raise. Not because I think it's wrong for wealthy nations to pursue enhancement—I don't—but because it represents a genuine ethical challenge we haven't adequately addressed. When one side of a conflict has access to enhancement technology and the other doesn't, we're not just talking about individual soldiers anymore. We're talking about structural advantages that could reshape global power dynamics for generations.

Still, I maintain that the benefits of research outweigh these concerns. Don't let the forces of darkness, ignorance, and fear turn us back from research. Instead, let us train—and yes, even enhance—new generations of capable soldiers, who can serve and protect in an increasingly complex and dangerous world.
